10. The Great Recession and the Covid-19 Pandemic: A First Look

Learning goals

Two shocks hit the world economy in less than 15 years: the global financial crisis of 2008–09 and the Covid-19 pandemic of 2020. This chapter looks at both in the data. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • tell the story of the financial crisis with data: the housing bubble, the Fed’s interest rate, the spreads between interest rates and the fall of the stock market;
  • compare the Covid-19 recession across countries, in lives lost and in GDP lost;
  • measure how deep the two recessions were (employment, short-run output, unemployment, Table 10.1) and describe the inflation that followed the pandemic;
  • derive the measurement tools behind the figures: average growth rates, the climb back after a crash, short-run output, the cumulative GDP loss, and the gap between log changes and percent changes;
  • use a balance sheet to derive how leverage magnifies returns, how small a fall in asset prices wipes out net worth, and why losses force asset sales; solve a simple model of a bank run;
  • read an interest rate spread as lenders’ fear of default, split a fall in GDP into the contributions of its components, and read the comparative statics of each result;
  • in Python: find peaks and troughs with idxmax and idxmin, shade recessions with one small function, reshape a table with melt, compare two vintages of the same data, and turn log changes into percent changes;
  • go beyond the textbook’s countries: pick any of up to 61 economies from long (tidy) data files, and spot breaks, gaps and changes of definition in international data.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

Model overview

This chapter has no new model to solve. It follows two recent recessions through the data: the global financial crisis of 2007–09, which began in the housing market and spread through the banks to the whole economy, and the Covid-19 pandemic of 2020, a sudden stop that was deeper but far shorter. What the chapter does add is a set of analytical tools. Some are measurement tools that every figure relies on: how far a series fell, how fast it grew, how long it took to climb back. Others come from financial economics. They explain how a fall in house prices of about a third could bring large banks to the edge of collapse: balance sheets, leverage, bank runs and interest rate spreads.

This section writes out each tool as a small framework, in the same three steps we use for a model: the definitions it starts from, the algebra that turns them into a result, and what the result predicts. We move from measurement to finance to macroeconomic outcomes: (i) booms, busts and recoveries; (ii) balance sheets and leverage; (iii) bank runs; (iv) interest rate spreads; (v) short-run output and the cost of a slump; (vi) the components of GDP in a recession; and (vii) the value of the lives the pandemic took. At the end, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each one with numbers, and ### Tools for comparing countries adds the helpers for the “Beyond the U.S.” charts. Every later section of the notebook reuses these functions.

As in the rest of the book, a bar over a letter marks a value we take as given, such as potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\), and a tilde marks short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\). The textbook describes balance sheets in words; to do the algebra we give each item a letter where it first appears. Inside formulas, rates are decimals (0.05); in the text and the charts they are percentages (5 percent).

Measuring booms, busts and recoveries

Definitions

Let \(X_t\) be any series observed at date \(t\): a price index, GDP, employment. Most figures compare an earlier date \(s\) with a later date \(t\). The percent change between them is

\[\%\Delta X = 100\times\left(\frac{X_t}{X_s}-1\right). \tag{1}\]

  • A peak is the highest value inside a window of dates, and a trough is the lowest value after that peak. The fall from peak to trough is equation (1) with \(s\) the peak and \(t\) the trough, so it is a negative number.
  • The drawdown at date \(t\) is the percent change from the highest value reached so far, \(100\times\left(X_t/\max_{s\le t}X_s - 1\right)\). It is zero at every new record (Fig. 1).
  • For a series that is itself a rate, such as the unemployment rate \(u_t\), an interest rate or an inflation rate, we report the difference \(u_t - u_s\) in percentage points. Unemployment that goes from 4 to 6 percent has risen by 2 points, but by 50 percent.
  • The NBER dates each recession by a peak, the last month of the expansion, and a trough, the last month of the recession. The number of months between two dates is \(12\times(\text{difference in years}) + (\text{difference in months})\).

Solving: four results we use again and again

Step 1: the average growth rate over many years. Suppose \(X\) grew at the same rate \(g\) in each of \(T\) years. Then \(X_T = X_0(1+g)^T\). Divide both sides by \(X_0\) and raise them to the power \(1/T\), using \(\left((1+g)^T\right)^{1/T} = 1+g\) (Appendix C.3):

\[g = \left(\frac{X_T}{X_0}\right)^{1/T}-1. \tag{2}\]

Logs give a handy shortcut. Since \(\ln(X_T/X_0) = T\ln(1+g)\) and \(\ln(1+g)\approx g\) when \(g\) is small (Appendix C.6), \(g \approx \ln(X_T/X_0)/T\). In our data, real U.S. house prices were 1.72 times higher in 2006 than in 1996 (Fig. 1). Equation (2) gives \(1.72^{1/10}-1 \approx 5.6\) percent a year, and the shortcut gives \(\ln 1.72/10 \approx 5.4\) percent. By the rule of 70, a price that grows at that pace doubles in about \(70/5.6 \approx 12.5\) years.

Step 2: the climb back after a fall. If a series falls by the fraction \(f\) from its peak, the trough is \(X_{\text{trough}} = (1-f)X_{\text{peak}}\). To get back to the peak, the series must be multiplied by \(X_{\text{peak}}/X_{\text{trough}} = 1/(1-f)\). Written as a percentage, and putting both terms over the common denominator \(1-f\), the rise needed is

\[\text{rise needed} = 100\times\left(\frac{1}{1-f}-\frac{1-f}{1-f}\right) = 100\times\frac{f}{1-f}. \tag{3}\]

After a small fall, the climb back is about as large as the fall. After a large fall it is much larger: a series that has lost half its value must double to recover.

Step 3: why a ratio scale. Figs. 1 and 4 use a ratio (log) scale. On it, the vertical distance between two values is \(\ln X_t - \ln X_s = \ln(X_t/X_s)\) (Appendix C.4), which depends only on their ratio. A fall by one half and a rise of 100 percent cover the same distance, \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\). That is why busts of different decades, at very different price levels, can be compared by eye.

Step 4: log changes and percent changes. The inflation data of Fig. 10 measure the 12-month change in the price level \(P_t\) as a log change, \(\pi^{\log}_t = 100\ln(P_t/P_{t-12})\), while the usual inflation rate is the percent change \(\pi_t = 100\times(P_t/P_{t-12}-1)\). To go from the first to the second, divide the log change by 100 and undo the log with the exponential function, \(P_t/P_{t-12} = e^{\pi^{\log}_t/100}\). Substituting this ratio into the percent change gives

\[\pi_t = 100\times\left(e^{\pi^{\log}_t/100}-1\right). \tag{4}\]

How large is the difference? The exponential function can be written as \(e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2 + \dots\), so \(\pi_t \approx \pi^{\log}_t + (\pi^{\log}_t)^2/200\). The gap grows with the square of inflation: about 0.02 points at 2 percent inflation, but about 0.4 points at 9 percent.

What the measures tell us

A fall of … needs a rise of … (equation 3) where it happened
10 percent 11.1 percent
25 percent 33.3 percent
35.7 percent 55.5 percent real U.S. house prices, Dec 2005 to Feb 2012 (Fig. 1)
51.7 percent 107 percent the real S&P 500, Oct 2007 to Mar 2009 (Fig. 4)
  • The rise needed in equation (3) grows faster than the fall: its slope with respect to \(f\) is \(1/(1-f)^2\), which is above one and increases with \(f\) (Appendix C.7). Deep crashes take a long time to undo, even when growth afterwards is strong.
  • Percent changes do not add up over time, but log changes do. A fall of 50 percent followed by a rise of 50 percent leaves a series 25 percent below its start, and indeed \(\ln 0.5 + \ln 1.5 = \ln 0.75\).
  • When inflation is low, log and percent changes are interchangeable. When it is high, as in 2022, the choice moves the peaks by about half a point (Fig. 10).

Balance sheets and leverage

Definitions and assumptions

A balance sheet is a snapshot, on one date, of what an institution owns and what it owes. It works the same way for a bank, a firm, a household or a government.

  • Assets \(A\) are what it owns (in this chapter \(A\) stands for assets, not for productivity). For a bank: loans, securities and other investments, and cash and reserves.
  • Liabilities \(D\) (for debt) are what it owes to others. For a bank: deposits, short-term debt and long-term debt.
  • Net worth \(E\), also called equity or capital, is what is left for the owners: assets minus liabilities. Because net worth is defined as that difference, the two sides of a balance sheet always match. The leverage ratio \(\ell\) counts the dollars borrowed per dollar of the owners’ own money:

\[A = D + E, \qquad \ell \equiv \frac{D}{E}. \tag{5}\]

Regulators watch two more ratios. The capital ratio \(E/A\) is the share of assets paid for by the owners, and a capital requirement sets a floor for it, for example 6 percent. The reserve ratio is cash and reserves divided by deposits, and a reserve requirement sets a floor for it, for example 3 percent.

The experiments below rest on one assumption: liabilities are promises to repay fixed dollar amounts, while the market value of assets moves with house prices, stock prices and defaults.

Our running example is the hypothetical bank of the textbook’s Table 10.3, in billions of dollars. Its assets are loans of 1,000, investments of 900 and cash and reserves of 100, so \(A = 2{,}000\). It owes 1,000 in deposits, 400 in short-term debt and 400 in long-term debt, so \(D = 1{,}800\) and \(E = 200\). Equation (5) gives \(\ell = 1{,}800/200 = 9\). Its capital ratio is \(200/2{,}000\) and its reserve ratio \(100/1{,}000\), both 10 percent, above the two floors.

Solving

Step 1: leverage and the capital ratio carry the same information. Divide both sides of \(A = D + E\) by \(E\):

\[\frac{A}{E} = \frac{D}{E} + 1 = 1 + \ell, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{E}{A} = \frac{1}{1+\ell}.\]

With \(\ell = 9\), every 10 dollars of assets rest on 1 dollar of equity. A capital requirement is therefore a ceiling on leverage: \(E/A \ge 0.06\) means \(1+\ell \le 1/0.06\), or \(\ell \le 15.7\).

Step 2: leverage magnifies returns. Let the value of the assets change by \(\Delta A\). The liabilities do not move, \(\Delta D = 0\), so the change in \(A = D + E\) is \(\Delta E = \Delta A\): every dollar gained or lost lands on the owners. Divide by \(E\), then multiply and divide by \(A\):

\[\frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{\Delta A}{E} = \frac{A}{E}\times\frac{\Delta A}{A} = (1+\ell)\,\frac{\Delta A}{A}. \tag{6}\]

The owners’ percent return is \(1+\ell\) times the percent return on all the assets. For our bank \(1+\ell = 10\), so a 1 percent gain on its assets, 20 billion dollars, raises its equity by 10 percent. When only one item changes, measure its change relative to total assets: a gain of 100 billion on the investments is \(100/2{,}000 = 5\) percent of all assets, and so 50 percent for the owners. Households work the same way. A buyer who pays 20 percent of the price of a house and borrows the other 80 percent has \(E/A = 0.2\), so \(1+\ell = 5\): each 1 percent change in the price of the house moves the owner’s equity by 5 percent, up or down.

Intuition. Lenders are paid first, and they are paid a fixed amount. The owners keep whatever is left: a thin layer on top of a large pile of debt. A small change in the size of the whole pile is a large change in the thickness of that layer.

Step 3: how small a fall wipes out the owners. Let the value of the assets fall by the fraction \(f\), so that \(A\) becomes \((1-f)A\) while \(D\) stays the same. Net worth becomes

\[E' = (1-f)A - D = (A - D) - fA = E - fA.\]

The owners are wiped out, \(E' \le 0\), as soon as \(fA \ge E\), that is, once the fall reaches

\[f^* = \frac{E}{A} = \frac{1}{1+\ell}. \tag{7}\]

Beyond that point the bank is insolvent, or bankrupt: even if it sold everything at market prices, it could not repay what it owes. With \(\ell = 9\), \(f^*\) is 10 percent. Bear Stearns had a leverage of about 35 when it collapsed in 2008, so \(f^* = 1/36\), about 2.8 percent.

Step 4: losses force sales (deleveraging). After a loss of \(x\) dollars, assets are \(A - x\) and equity is \(E - x\), so leverage jumps to \(D/(E-x)\), above \(\ell\). Suppose the bank wants, or its regulators require, to bring leverage back to \(\ell\), and it cannot raise new equity. Then its assets must shrink to \((1+\ell)(E-x)\): it sells assets and uses the cash to repay debt. The sales needed are the assets left after the loss minus that target. Expanding, and using \(A = (1+\ell)E\) from Step 1:

\[(A - x) - (1+\ell)(E - x) = A - x - (1+\ell)E + (1+\ell)x = \ell\,x. \tag{8}\]

Each dollar of losses forces \(\ell\) dollars of asset sales: 9 for our bank, 35 for Bear Stearns.

Intuition. When many leveraged banks sell the same kind of assets at the same time, the prices of those assets fall further. That causes new losses, and equation (8) turns them into new sales. Through this loop, losses on subprime mortgages, small next to the total wealth of the United States, could shake the whole financial system.

What the model predicts

Higher leverage \(\ell\) means … formula sign at \(\ell = 9\) at \(\ell = 35\)
a bigger multiplier on the owners’ returns \(1+\ell\), equation (6) \(+\) 10 36
a smaller fall that wipes out equity \(1/(1+\ell)\), equation (7) \(-\) 10 percent 2.8 percent
more forced sales per dollar of losses \(\ell\), equation (8) \(+\) 9 35
  • As an elasticity, equation (6) says that net worth responds to the value of assets with elasticity \(A/E = 1+\ell\). Taking logs of equation (7), \(\ln f^* = -\ln(1+\ell)\): doubling \(1+\ell\) halves the cushion.
  • The multiplier works in both directions. When asset prices rise, a 5 percent gain becomes 50 percent for the owners; when they fall, the same multiplier turns small losses into bankruptcies.
  • Households are exposed in the same way. With an 80 percent mortgage, \(\ell = 4\), and equation (7) says a fall of 20 percent in the price of the house wipes out the owner’s equity; any further fall leaves the house worth less than the mortgage. Lost housing wealth helps explain why consumption fell in the Great Recession (see the components of GDP below).
  • Who holds the losses matters. Losses spread over millions of unleveraged shareholders, like the dot-com crash of 2000–03, hurt but do not bankrupt anyone; similar losses concentrated in a few highly leveraged banks do (Fig. 4).

Bank runs and liquidity crises

Assumptions

  • The bank’s assets come in two kinds. Liquid assets, cash and reserves \(R\), can be paid out at full value at once. Illiquid assets, the loans and most investments, are worth their full value if the bank keeps them. Sold in a hurry, each dollar of them brings only \(1-\delta\) dollars of cash, where the fire-sale discount \(\delta\) is between 0 and 1.
  • Depositors may take their money out at any time. Suppose they withdraw \(W\) dollars.

Solving the model

If \(W \le R\), the bank pays out of its cash and nothing else happens. If \(W > R\), it needs \(W - R\) more cash, so it sells illiquid assets with a book value \(S\) such that \((1-\delta)S = W - R\). Solving for \(S\) gives \(S = (W-R)/(1-\delta)\). The bank gives up assets worth \(S\) but receives only \((1-\delta)S\) in cash, so it loses the difference \(\delta S\):

\[\text{loss} = \delta S = \frac{\delta\,(W-R)}{1-\delta}. \tag{9}\]

The loss comes out of net worth, which falls to \(E - \delta(W-R)/(1-\delta)\). The run bankrupts the bank when the loss is larger than \(E\). We can solve this condition in two directions.

  • How large a discount bankrupts the bank in a full run? If every depositor leaves, \(W\) is equal to total deposits. Set the loss equal to \(E\) and solve for \(\delta\): \(\delta(W-R) = E(1-\delta)\), so \(\delta(W-R+E) = E\) and \[\delta^* = \frac{E}{E + W - R}.\] For our bank, \(\delta^* = 200/(200 + 1{,}000 - 100) = 200/1{,}100\), about 18 percent.
  • How large a run bankrupts the bank at a given discount? Solve the same condition for \(W\) instead: \(W^* = R + E(1-\delta)/\delta\). With a discount of one quarter, \(W^* = 100 + 200\times 0.75/0.25 = 700\). A run on 70 percent of the deposits is enough.

What the model predicts

  • Runs can be self-fulfilling. At normal prices the bank is solvent. But if each depositor expects the others to run, running first is the best thing to do, and the forced sales then make the bank insolvent. The same bank survives or fails depending only on what depositors expect.
  • Illiquid is not the same as insolvent. Without a run, \(\delta\) never matters. The fire-sale discount is what turns a liquidity problem into a solvency problem.
  • Comparative statics. A run is harder to trigger, \(W^*\) is larger, when the bank holds more liquid assets \(R\), has more equity \(E\) or faces a smaller discount \(\delta\). Each policy works on one of these: capital requirements raise \(E\), reserve requirements raise \(R\), and a central bank that lends against illiquid assets, the lender of last resort, spares the bank the fire sale. Deposit insurance, run by the FDIC in the United States since 1933, takes away the reason to run in the first place.
  • In 2007–08 the runs hit mostly the short-term debt of banks and investment banks. Unlike insured deposits, those loans could simply not be renewed. When lenders pull back across a whole market at once, the volume of lending dries up: a liquidity crisis.

Interest rate spreads: a thermometer of fear

Definitions

An interest rate spread is the difference between the interest rate on a risky loan, \(i\), and the rate on a safe one, \(i^f\), measured in percentage points. The TED spread of Fig. 3 is the 3-month LIBOR rate, at which banks lent to one another, minus the 3-month Treasury bill rate, at which the U.S. government borrows.

Solving: what a spread measures

A lender with one dollar can buy a Treasury bill, which pays \(1 + i^f\) for sure. Or it can lend to another bank, which pays \(1+i\) if the borrower survives, with probability \(1-p\), and in the simplest case nothing if it fails. A lender who cares only about the expected payoff is willing to lend to the bank when the two options pay the same on average:

\[(1-p)(1+i) = 1+i^f.\]

Divide by \(1-p\), subtract \(1+i^f\) from both sides and factor out \(1+i^f\):

\[i - i^f = \frac{1+i^f}{1-p} - (1+i^f) = (1+i^f)\left(\frac{1}{1-p}-1\right) = \frac{(1+i^f)\,p}{1-p} \approx p. \tag{10}\]

The approximation holds when \(p\) and \(i^f\) are both small, so that \(1+i^f \approx 1\) and \(1-p\approx 1\). The spread is then roughly the probability of default, as lenders see it. A spread of a third of a point, typical of the calm years before 2007, corresponds to a perceived default risk of about 0.3 percent a year. The monthly peak of the TED spread, about 3.35 points in October 2008, corresponds to about 3.2 percent: ten times more fear.

What the model predicts

  • The spread rises almost one for one with perceived default risk: its slope with respect to \(p\) is \((1+i^f)/(1-p)^2\), close to 1.
  • If lenders get part of their money back when a borrower fails, the spread is smaller for the same \(p\). If they dislike risk, they ask for more than equation (10). Either way the spread moves with the fear of default.
  • Flight to safety. When fear rises, lenders leave interbank loans for Treasury bills. That pushes \(i^f\) down and \(i\) up, so the spread widens from both sides.
  • Banks that worry about their own funding also hoard cash rather than lend it, which adds a liquidity premium on top of the default premium. A spread that jumps is a sign of a liquidity crisis (Fig. 3).

Short-run output and the cost of a slump

Definitions

Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) is the GDP the economy would produce with its resources in normal use; for the United States the Congressional Budget Office estimates it. Short-run output (Chapter 9) is the percent gap between actual GDP \(Y_t\) and potential:

\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t}, \tag{11}\]

shown in percent in the charts. Rearranged, \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t(1+\tilde{Y}_t)\): a value of \(-0.05\) means that GDP is 5 percent below potential. The OECD calls the same measure the output gap.

Solving

Step 1: in logs. Take logs of \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t(1+\tilde{Y}_t)\) and use \(\ln(1+x)\approx x\) (Appendix C.6):

\[\ln Y_t = \ln\bar{Y}_t + \ln(1+\tilde{Y}_t) \approx \ln\bar{Y}_t + \tilde{Y}_t.\]

Short-run output is approximately log GDP minus log potential output.

Step 2: growth and the gap. Write this equation for two consecutive years and subtract. A difference in logs is a growth rate (Appendix C.5), so

\[g_{Y,t} \approx \bar{g}_t + \Delta\tilde{Y}_t,\]

where \(\bar{g}_t\) is the growth rate of potential output. To close a negative gap, GDP must grow faster than potential. Closing a gap of 5 percent in five years takes growth one point a year above potential, every year. Growth only a little above potential closes the gap slowly, which is why \(\tilde{Y}\) stayed negative for most of the 2010s (Fig. 8).

Step 3: the cumulative loss. Fig. 5 measures the pandemic’s GDP loss against the pre-pandemic level \(Y_0\) of 2019Q4, not against potential. Write real GDP in quarter \(q\) as an index, \(I_q = 100\,Y_q/Y_0\). Quarterly GDP is reported at an annual rate, so a quarter produces one fourth of that rate. The output lost in quarter \(q\), as a share of one year’s GDP, is therefore \((Y_0 - Y_q)/(4Y_0) = (100 - I_q)/400\), or \((100 - I_q)/4\) in percent. Quarters above the old level count as no loss. Adding up from 2020Q1:

\[\text{GDP loss} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{q}\max\left(0,\;100 - I_q\right), \tag{12}\]

in percent of one year’s GDP. The same sum with \(-100\,\tilde{Y}_q\) in place of \(100 - I_q\) measures the loss against potential output instead.

What it predicts

  • Depth times duration. If output drops by \(d\) percent at once and climbs back in a straight line over \(T\) years, the sum in equation (12) is close to the area of a triangle, \(\tfrac{1}{2}dT\). A slump twice as deep costs twice as much, and so does a slump twice as long.
  • So a deep but short slump can cost less than a moderate but long one. Against potential, the Great Recession pushed \(\tilde{Y}\) to about \(-5\) percent and kept it below zero for about nine years: a triangle of about \(\tfrac{1}{2}\times5\times9 \approx 22\) percent of a year’s GDP. The 2020 slump, near \(-9\) percent but over within about a year, gives a triangle of about 4. ### The model in code computes the exact sums with the data.
  • Potential output is an estimate, and GDP is revised for years. Both change \(\tilde{Y}\), as the two vintages of Fig. 8 show.

The components of GDP in a recession

Definitions

The national income identity of Chapter 2 splits GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, exports and imports:

\[Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + EX_t - IM_t.\]

The share of a component \(X\) in GDP is \(X/Y\), measured at the peak of the recession.

Solving

Between the peak and the trough the identity holds in changes: \(\Delta Y = \Delta C + \Delta I + \Delta G + \Delta EX - \Delta IM\). Divide both sides by \(Y\), and write each term as a share times a percent change, for example \(\Delta C/Y = (C/Y)\times(\Delta C/C)\):

\[\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \frac{C}{Y}\frac{\Delta C}{C} + \frac{I}{Y}\frac{\Delta I}{I} + \frac{G}{Y}\frac{\Delta G}{G} + \frac{EX}{Y}\frac{\Delta EX}{EX} - \frac{IM}{Y}\frac{\Delta IM}{IM}. \tag{13}\]

Each term is a contribution to GDP growth, in percentage points: the component’s share times its own percent change. Table 10.1 reports the percent changes; the contributions show which of them moved GDP the most.

What it predicts

  • A small component that swings a lot can matter more than a large one that barely moves. Investment is only about a sixth of GDP, but it fell by almost 30 percent between the quarterly peak and trough of the Great Recession. Its contribution, close to \(-5\) points, is larger than the whole fall in GDP. Consumption is two thirds of GDP, so even its fall of about 2 percent subtracted about 1.5 points.
  • Imports enter with a minus sign. A fall in imports adds to GDP growth, because part of what households and firms stopped buying had been made abroad.
  • In most recessions consumption hardly moves, because households smooth consumption: they base it on their long-run (permanent) income rather than on this year’s income (Chapter 16). In 2008–09 the falls in house and stock prices cut household wealth, and with it permanent income, so consumption fell. In 2020 people stayed away from shops, restaurants and travel, and consumption led the fall.
  • Real GDP is measured in chained dollars, which do not add up exactly, so the contributions miss GDP growth by a small residual.

Lives lost and their value

Definitions

  • Deaths are counted per million people, \(m\). The mortality rate is \(m/10^6\), and “one out of every \(X\) people” means \(X = 10^6/m\).
  • The value of a statistical life \(V\) is the amount society is willing to pay, on average, to avoid one death. Agencies such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency use it to weigh safety rules against their cost. A person of middle age has about \(T\) years of life ahead.

Solving

The simplest approach spreads \(V\) evenly over the remaining years, so a year of life is worth \(v = V/T\). Losing \(\Delta\) years of life expectancy then costs about \(\Delta\times v\) per person (the key numbers of Fig. 5).

Years far in the future usually count for less (Appendix C.12). If \(V\) is the present value of \(T\) equal yearly values \(v\), discounted at the rate \(r\), then by the sum of a geometric series

\[V = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{v}{(1+r)^t} = v\,\frac{1-(1+r)^{-T}}{r}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad v = \frac{r\,V}{1-(1+r)^{-T}}.\]

With \(V = 10\) million dollars, \(T = 40\) years and \(r = 0.03\), a year of life is worth about 433,000 dollars, against 250,000 without discounting.

What it predicts

  • The value of a year of life rises with \(V\) and falls with \(T\). Discounting raises it: later years count for less, so for the same \(V\) each year must be worth more.
  • Even without discounting, the value of the life expectancy lost in the pandemic is many times the lost output of equation (12), which for the United States was a few percent of one year’s income per person.

The model in code

We now turn the results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes, and the cells after the functions check the algebra above with numbers. The first functions measure changes in any series.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. For a pandas Series with dates as row labels, series[start:end] keeps the rows between two dates, .idxmax() gives the date of the largest value and .idxmin() the date of the smallest. A function can return several results at once, separated by commas.

def percent_change(new, old):
    """Percent change from old to new: 100 (new / old - 1)   (equation 1)."""
    return 100 * (new / old - 1)


def peak_to_trough(series, start, end):
    """The highest point between start and end, the lowest point after it, and the fall in percent."""
    window = series[start:end]
    peak = window.idxmax()                      # date of the highest value
    trough = window[peak:].idxmin()             # date of the lowest value after the peak
    return peak, trough, percent_change(window[trough], window[peak])


def low_to_high(series, start, end):
    """The opposite measure: the highest point between start and end, the lowest point before it, and the rise."""
    window = series[start:end]
    high = window.idxmax()                      # date of the highest value
    low = window[:high].idxmin()                # date of the lowest value before it
    return low, high, window[high] - window[low]

For a series that rises in a recession, such as the unemployment rate, low_to_high measures the rise from the lowest point to the highest one, in the units of the series (percentage points for a rate). Two more functions compute equations (2) and (3).

Python note. ** means “to the power of”, and np.log is the natural logarithm. An f-string such as f"g = {x:.2f}" writes the value of x into the text; :.2f shows two decimals and :+.1f one decimal with its sign.

def annual_growth(factor, years):
    """Average growth rate per year when a series is multiplied by `factor` in `years` years (equation 2)."""
    return factor ** (1 / years) - 1


def rise_needed(fall):
    """Percent rise needed to undo a fall by the fraction `fall`: 100 f / (1 - f)   (equation 3)."""
    return 100 * fall / (1 - fall)

Check 1: the measurement tools. Compound the growth rate of equation (2) for 10 years and see whether we get the factor back. Then let a series fall and rise by the amount equation (3) gives. Last, take a price level that rises by 9 percent and compute both inflation measures and equation (4).

Python note. A for loop repeats its indented lines once for each element of a list. np.exp is the exponential function \(e^x\).

factor, years = 1.72, 10                         # real house prices, 1996 to 2006 (Fig. 1)
g = annual_growth(factor, years)
print(f"Equation (2): g = {100 * g:.2f}% a year;  shortcut ln(factor) / T = {100 * np.log(factor) / years:.2f}%")
print(f"Compounded for 10 years: (1 + g)^10 = {(1 + g) ** years:.4f}   (the factor was {factor})")

for fall in [0.10, 0.357, 0.517]:
    rise = rise_needed(fall)
    back = 100 * (1 - fall) * (1 + rise / 100)   # start at 100, fall, then rise
    print(f"Fall {100 * fall:4.1f}%: rise needed {rise:5.1f}%;  100 -> {100 * (1 - fall):.1f} -> {back:.1f}")

ratio = 1.09                                     # prices 9% higher than 12 months earlier
log_change = 100 * np.log(ratio)
print(f"Log change {log_change:.3f}; percent change {100 * (ratio - 1):.3f}; equation (4) gives "
      f"{100 * (np.exp(log_change / 100) - 1):.3f}; approximation {log_change + log_change ** 2 / 200:.3f}")
Equation (2): g = 5.57% a year;  shortcut ln(factor) / T = 5.42%
Compounded for 10 years: (1 + g)^10 = 1.7200   (the factor was 1.72)
Fall 10.0%: rise needed  11.1%;  100 -> 90.0 -> 100.0
Fall 35.7%: rise needed  55.5%;  100 -> 64.3 -> 100.0
Fall 51.7%: rise needed 107.0%;  100 -> 48.3 -> 100.0
Log change 8.618; percent change 9.000; equation (4) gives 9.000; approximation 8.989

Recessions. Five figures shade the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month), and the same dates in quarters. One small function adds the shaded bands to any figure.

Python note. parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands the loop one (peak, trough) pair at a time. The if skips recessions that ended before the chart starts, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates.

recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv",
                         parse_dates=["peak", "trough", "peak_quarter", "trough_quarter"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start="2000-01-01"):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after `start` (Figs. 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    return fig


recessions.tail(3)
peak trough peak_quarter trough_quarter
8 2001-03-01 2001-11-01 2001-01-01 2001-10-01
9 2007-12-01 2009-06-01 2007-10-01 2009-04-01
10 2020-02-01 2020-04-01 2019-10-01 2020-04-01

The Great Recession runs from the peak in December 2007 to the trough in June 2009, and the Covid-19 recession from February to April 2020, only two months.

Balance sheets. The hypothetical bank of Table 10.3 (billions of dollars) is a small table, and two functions compute equation (5).

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary, a set of key: value pairs in curly braces. .sum() adds up all the values. In an f-string, {x:,} adds thousands separators and {x:.0f} rounds to 0 decimals.

def net_worth(assets, liabilities):
    """Equity (net worth) E = A - D   (equation 5)."""
    return assets - liabilities


def leverage(liabilities, equity):
    """Leverage ratio = D / E   (equation 5)."""
    return liabilities / equity


assets = pd.Series({"Loans": 1000, "Investments": 900, "Cash and reserves": 100})
liabilities = pd.Series({"Deposits": 1000, "Short-term debt": 400, "Long-term debt": 400})
equity = net_worth(assets.sum(), liabilities.sum())
print(f"Total assets {assets.sum():,}, total liabilities {liabilities.sum():,}, net worth {equity:,}")
print(f"Leverage = {liabilities.sum():,} / {equity} = {leverage(liabilities.sum(), equity):.0f}")
print(f"Capital ratio = {100 * equity / assets.sum():.0f}% of assets; reserves = "
      f"{100 * assets['Cash and reserves'] / liabilities['Deposits']:.0f}% of deposits")
Total assets 2,000, total liabilities 1,800, net worth 200
Leverage = 1,800 / 200 = 9
Capital ratio = 10% of assets; reserves = 10% of deposits

Check 2: leverage magnifies gains and losses (equation 6). Let the investments gain or lose value. The liabilities do not change, so all of the gain or loss lands on net worth:

for new_investments in [1000, 600]:
    new_equity = net_worth(assets.sum() - assets["Investments"] + new_investments, liabilities.sum())
    print(f"Investments {assets['Investments']} -> {new_investments}: return "
          f"{percent_change(new_investments, assets['Investments']):+.1f}%, net worth {equity} -> {new_equity}, "
          f"return to the owners {percent_change(new_equity, equity):+.1f}%")
Investments 900 -> 1000: return +11.1%, net worth 200 -> 300, return to the owners +50.0%
Investments 900 -> 600: return -33.3%, net worth 200 -> -100, return to the owners -150.0%

A gain of 100 is 5 percent of total assets and becomes a gain of 50 percent for the owners, \(1+\ell = 10\) times as much. A loss of 300, only 15 percent of total assets, is more than the 10 percent cushion of equation (7): net worth turns negative and the bank is insolvent. The same arithmetic works for a house bought for 500,000 dollars with 20 percent down, where \(1+\ell = 5\):

house, mortgage = 500_000, 400_000
for price_change in [10, -10, -20]:
    new_equity = net_worth(house * (1 + price_change / 100), mortgage)
    print(f"House price {price_change:+d}%: equity {house - mortgage:,} -> {new_equity:,.0f} "
          f"({percent_change(new_equity, house - mortgage):+.0f}%)")
House price +10%: equity 100,000 -> 150,000 (+50%)
House price -10%: equity 100,000 -> 50,000 (-50%)
House price -20%: equity 100,000 -> 0 (-100%)

Check 3: the cushion and forced sales (equations 7 and 8). Raise all assets by 1 percent and compare with equation (6). Then let them fall by exactly \(f^* = 1/(1+\ell)\): net worth should be zero. Last, give the bank a loss of 10 and let it sell assets until leverage is back at 9: equation (8) says it must sell \(9\times10 = 90\).

A, D = assets.sum(), liabilities.sum()
L = leverage(D, equity)
print(f"Assets +1%: net worth changes by {percent_change(net_worth(1.01 * A, D), equity):+.1f}%;  "
      f"equation (6): {(1 + L) * 1:+.1f}%")
for L_bank in [L, 35]:
    f_star = 1 / (1 + L_bank)
    E_bank = A / (1 + L_bank)                    # a bank of the same size with leverage L_bank
    left = net_worth((1 - f_star) * A, A - E_bank)
    print(f"Leverage {L_bank:.0f}: wipe-out fall {100 * f_star:.1f}%; net worth after that fall {left:.1f}")

x = 10                                           # a loss of 10 billion dollars
sales = (A - x) - (1 + L) * (equity - x)         # assets after the loss minus the target
new_A, new_D = A - x - sales, D - sales          # the cash from the sales repays debt
print(f"Loss {x}: sales needed {sales:.0f} (equation (8): {L * x:.0f}); "
      f"leverage after the sales {leverage(new_D, net_worth(new_A, new_D)):.1f}")
Assets +1%: net worth changes by +10.0%;  equation (6): +10.0%
Leverage 9: wipe-out fall 10.0%; net worth after that fall 0.0
Leverage 35: wipe-out fall 2.8%; net worth after that fall 0.0
Loss 10: sales needed 90 (equation (8): 90); leverage after the sales 9.0

Check 4: a bank run (equation 9). We let the bank’s depositors withdraw more and more, with a fire-sale discount of 25 percent, and compute the loss and the net worth that is left. Then we confirm the two thresholds: a full run at the discount \(\delta^*\), and a run of size \(W^*\) at the discount of 25 percent, should both cost exactly the bank’s net worth.

Python note. if ... : runs its indented lines only when the condition is true; a bare return inside it leaves the function early with that result.

def run_loss(withdrawals, cash, discount):
    """Loss from selling illiquid assets at a discount to pay withdrawals beyond the cash (equation 9)."""
    if withdrawals <= cash:
        return 0.0
    return discount * (withdrawals - cash) / (1 - discount)


R, deposits = assets["Cash and reserves"], liabilities["Deposits"]
for W in [100, 400, 700, 1000]:
    loss = run_loss(W, R, 0.25)
    print(f"Withdrawals {W:5,}: loss {loss:6.1f}, net worth left {equity - loss:7.1f}")

d_star = equity / (equity + deposits - R)
W_star = R + equity * (1 - 0.25) / 0.25
print(f"Full run: critical discount {100 * d_star:.1f}%, loss {run_loss(deposits, R, d_star):.1f} = net worth {equity}")
print(f"Discount 25%: critical run {W_star:.0f} ({100 * W_star / deposits:.0f}% of deposits), "
      f"loss {run_loss(W_star, R, 0.25):.1f} = net worth {equity}")
Withdrawals   100: loss    0.0, net worth left   200.0
Withdrawals   400: loss  100.0, net worth left   100.0
Withdrawals   700: loss  200.0, net worth left     0.0
Withdrawals 1,000: loss  300.0, net worth left  -100.0
Full run: critical discount 18.2%, loss 200.0 = net worth 200
Discount 25%: critical run 700 (70% of deposits), loss 200.0 = net worth 200

Check 5: spreads and default risk (equation 10). For two default probabilities, we compute the loan rate that makes a lender indifferent, with a safe rate of 1 percent. The expected payoff of the loan must equal the T-bill’s, and the spread should be close to \(p\).

i_safe = 0.01
for p in [0.003, 0.032]:
    i_loan = (1 + i_safe) / (1 - p) - 1          # from (1 - p)(1 + i) = 1 + i_safe
    print(f"Default probability {100 * p:.1f}%: loan rate {100 * i_loan:.2f}%, spread {100 * (i_loan - i_safe):.2f} "
          f"points; expected payoff {(1 - p) * (1 + i_loan):.4f} vs T-bill {1 + i_safe:.4f}")
Default probability 0.3%: loan rate 1.30%, spread 0.30 points; expected payoff 1.0100 vs T-bill 1.0100
Default probability 3.2%: loan rate 4.34%, spread 3.34 points; expected payoff 1.0100 vs T-bill 1.0100

Check 6: the cumulative GDP loss (equation 12). First a made-up slump: output drops by 8 percent at once and climbs back in a straight line over 2 years (8 quarters). The triangle rule gives \(\tfrac12\times8\times2 = 8\). Then the real thing: the loss against potential output, from short-run output in the data of Fig. 8.

Python note. np.linspace(92, 100, 9) gives 9 evenly spaced numbers from 92 to 100. np.maximum(a, 0) replaces every negative number by 0, so quarters above the old level count as no loss.

def gdp_loss(index):
    """Cumulative GDP loss in percent of one year's GDP; index = 100 at the old level (equation 12)."""
    return np.maximum(100 - index, 0).sum() / 4


path = np.linspace(92, 100, 9)                   # 2019Q4 = 100, then 92 at the trough, back to 100 after 8 quarters
print(f"Straight-line slump: equation (12) gives {gdp_loss(path):.2f}; the triangle rule gives {0.5 * 8 * 2:.2f}")

short_run = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig10-8.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date").short_run_output
for name, start, end in [("Great Recession", "2008-01-01", "2017-12-01"), ("Covid-19", "2020-01-01", "2021-12-01")]:
    window = short_run[start:end]
    print(f"{name}: lowest short-run output {window.min():.1f}%; "
          f"loss against potential {gdp_loss(100 + window):.1f}% of a year's GDP")
Straight-line slump: equation (12) gives 9.00; the triangle rule gives 8.00
Great Recession: lowest short-run output -5.0%; loss against potential 21.3% of a year's GDP
Covid-19: lowest short-run output -8.8%; loss against potential 3.4% of a year's GDP

The sum is 9, not 8: with quarterly steps, the first quarter at the trough counts in full, which adds the depth times half a quarter of a year, \(8\times\tfrac18 = 1\). In the data the Great Recession cost about 21 percent of a year’s GDP against potential, more than six times the 3.4 percent of the Covid-19 slump, close to the triangles of about 22 and 4.

Check 7: the contributions of the components (equation 13). We take real GDP and its components at the quarterly NBER peak and trough of each recession, from the file us_quarterly.csv that Table 10.1 uses. The contributions should add up to the change in GDP, apart from a small residual.

Python note. .set_index("date") makes the dates the row labels, and .loc["2007-10-01"] picks the row of one date. SIGN.items() hands the loop each key and its value; imports get the sign \(-1\).

components = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_quarterly.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
SIGN = {"consumption": 1, "investment": 1, "government": 1, "exports": 1, "imports": -1}
for name, peak, trough in [("Great Recession", "2007-10-01", "2009-04-01"), ("Covid-19", "2019-10-01", "2020-04-01")]:
    before, after = components.loc[peak], components.loc[trough]
    print(f"{name}: GDP {percent_change(after.gdp, before.gdp):+.2f}%")
    total = 0
    for part, sign in SIGN.items():
        share = 100 * before[part] / before.gdp
        change = percent_change(after[part], before[part])
        contribution = sign * share * change / 100
        total = total + contribution
        print(f"   {part:12} share {share:4.1f}%, change {change:+6.1f}%, contribution {contribution:+.2f} points")
    print(f"   sum of the contributions {total:+.2f} points")

   consumption  share 67.0%, change   -2.3%, contribution -1.51 points
   investment   share 16.3%, change  -29.3%, contribution -4.79 points
   government   share 19.9%, change   +5.3%, contribution +1.05 points
   exports      share 10.7%, change   -9.2%, contribution -0.99 points
   imports      share 14.0%, change  -17.9%, contribution +2.50 points
   sum of the contributions -3.74 points
Covid-19: GDP -9.09%
   consumption  share 67.3%, change  -10.2%, contribution -6.86 points
   investment   share 18.0%, change  -16.1%, contribution -2.89 points
   government   share 17.4%, change   +3.3%, contribution +0.57 points
   exports      share 11.8%, change  -23.9%, contribution -2.82 points
   imports      share 14.5%, change  -19.9%, contribution +2.88 points
   sum of the contributions -9.13 points

In the Great Recession, investment alone subtracted 4.8 points from GDP, more than the whole fall of 3.8 percent, and falling imports added 2.5 points back. In 2020, consumption subtracted 6.9 of the 9.1 points. The contributions miss GDP growth by less than 0.1 points.

Check 8: the value of a year of life. We compute \(v\) with and without discounting, and then add up the present value of 40 years at the discounted \(v\), one year at a time: it should give back the 10 million dollars.

Python note. range(1, T + 1) counts 1, 2, …, T. total = total + ... adds one more term to the sum on each pass of the loop.

V, T, r = 10e6, 40, 0.03
v_simple = V / T
v_discounted = r * V / (1 - (1 + r) ** -T)
present_value = 0
for t in range(1, T + 1):
    present_value = present_value + v_discounted / (1 + r) ** t
print(f"Value of a year of life: {v_simple:,.0f} dollars without discounting, {v_discounted:,.0f} at 3%")
print(f"Present value of {T} years at {v_discounted:,.0f}: {present_value:,.0f} dollars")
Value of a year of life: 250,000 dollars without discounting, 432,624 at 3%
Present value of 40 years at 432,624: 10,000,000 dollars

Tools for comparing countries

The textbook’s figures show the United States, and two of them the U.K. and the euro area. But the financial crisis and the pandemic hit the whole world, and the same data exist for many other economies: the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) collects house prices and central bank interest rates, the OECD unemployment, employment, stock prices and output gaps, and the IMF and Eurostat consumer prices. Most figures below therefore get a “Beyond the U.S.” part, where you pick the countries. Each of those data files is long: one row per country and date. The small file countries.csv lists every economy with its region.

countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
countries.head()
iso3 country region
0 ARG Argentina Americas
1 AUS Australia Asia and Pacific
2 AUT Austria Europe
3 BEL Belgium Europe
4 BRA Brazil Americas

A country should keep its color in every chart, so we give each one a fixed color once. The textbook’s economies keep the chapter’s colors.

Python note. enumerate(...) hands over each country name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % len(PALETTE) is the remainder of the division, so the positions cycle through the list of colors. .update({...}) overwrites some entries of a dictionary.

PALETTE = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet + px.colors.qualitative.Light24
COUNTRY_COLORS = {}
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    COUNTRY_COLORS[name] = PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)]
COUNTRY_COLORS.update({"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": GREEN, "Euro area": TEAL,
                       "S. Korea": "#5aa0d8", "Sweden": ORANGE, "Germany": "#0b4f47"})

Three small functions do the work in every “Beyond the U.S.” chart. pick keeps the rows of the chosen countries and lists the chosen countries that have no data. largest_fall and largest_rise apply peak_to_trough and low_to_high to each chosen country and report the most extreme one.

Python note. panel.country.isin(names) is true for the rows of the chosen countries, and panel[column].notna() for the rows with a value; & requires both. for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country") visits one country at a time, with rows holding its rows. None means “nothing found yet”. ", ".join(missing) glues a list of names into one text, separated by commas. In a Plotly title, <br> starts a new line and <sup>...</sup> writes smaller text.

def pick(panel, names, column):
    """Rows of the chosen countries that have a value in `column`, and the chosen countries without data."""
    chosen = panel[panel.country.isin(names) & panel[column].notna()]
    missing = []
    for name in names:
        if name not in set(chosen.country):
            missing.append(name)
    return chosen, missing


def no_data_note(missing):
    """A second, smaller title line that names the chosen countries without data."""
    if missing:
        return "<br><sup>No data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"
    return ""
def largest_fall(chosen, column, start, end):
    """Among the chosen countries, the largest peak-to-trough fall between start and end."""
    worst = None
    for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country"):
        series = rows.set_index("date")[column]
        if len(series[start:end]) > 1:
            peak, trough, change = peak_to_trough(series, start, end)
            if worst is None or change < worst[3]:
                worst = (name, peak, trough, change)
    return worst                                # (country, peak date, trough date, percent change)


def largest_rise(chosen, column, start, end):
    """Among the chosen countries, the largest rise from a low to a later high between start and end."""
    most = None
    for name, rows in chosen.groupby("country"):
        series = rows.set_index("date")[column]
        if len(series[start:end]) > 1:
            low, high, rise = low_to_high(series, start, end)
            if most is None or rise > most[3]:
                most = (name, low, high, rise)
    return most                                 # (country, low date, high date, rise in points)

The website cannot run Python, so its versions of these charts draw every country at once and show only the textbook’s countries; a click on a name in the legend adds a country, and a menu shows one region at a time. The next helper sets that up. Run it and move on.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions with all countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def all_countries(make_figure, names, shown):
    """Draw make_figure(names) for every country; show only `shown` and add a menu by region."""
    fig = make_figure(tuple(names))
    fig.update_layout(title=make_figure(tuple(shown)).layout.title)      # the title of the textbook's view
    region = dict(zip(countries.country, countries.region))
    choices = [("Textbook's view", list(shown)), ("All countries", list(names))]
    for r in ["Americas", "Europe", "Asia and Pacific", "Africa and Middle East"]:
        choices.append((r, [n for n in names if region.get(n) == r]))
    buttons = []
    for label, members in choices:
        visible = [True if t.name in members else "legendonly" for t in fig.data]
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace in fig.data:
        trace.visible = True if trace.name in shown else "legendonly"
        # a lighter page: the country name once in the hover text instead of once per point, months without the
        # day and time, and values rounded to 2 decimals
        trace.hovertemplate = trace.hovertemplate.replace("%{hovertext}", trace.name)
        trace.hovertext = None
        if trace.x is not None and len(trace.x) > 0 and hasattr(trace.x[0], "strftime"):
            trace.x = [d.strftime("%Y-%m") for d in pd.to_datetime(trace.x)]
        trace.y = np.round(np.asarray(trace.y, dtype=float), 2)
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True, tickmode="auto")                  # the y-axis follows the visible countries
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), legend=dict(title_text="Click to add"),
                      updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", direction="down", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left",
                                        yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons, showactive=True)])
    return fig

The Great Recession of 2007–2009

The financial crisis in four pictures: a boom and bust in house prices, the Fed’s interest rate, the stress between banks, and the stock market crash.

Fig. 1: A bursting bubble in U.S. housing prices?

Goal. Measure the boom and bust in U.S. house prices that started the financial crisis.

Robert Shiller’s index measures the price of a typical U.S. house, divided by the consumer price index so that it is in real terms, with 1953 = 100. We read it with dates as row labels, as a Series called house.

Python note. set_index("date") makes the dates the row labels, and .real_home_price_index then picks one column as a Series. .tail() shows the last five rows.

housing = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig10-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
house = housing.set_index("date").real_home_price_index
housing.tail()
date real_home_price_index
878 2026-03-01 186.726
879 2026-04-01 186.689
880 2026-05-01 186.867
881 2026-06-01 188.396
882 2026-07-01 188.778

The index has one value per month from January 1953 to July 2026. Each boom and bust gets a search window, and peak_to_trough finds the peak and trough inside it.

Python note. BUSTS is a dictionary: each name (the key) gives a pair of dates (the value), and BUSTS[bust] looks one up. start, end = ... unpacks the pair into two variables. px.line draws the index as a line, and log_y=True gives the ratio scale. fig.add_vrect shades the bust, and fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...)) adds the two black dots for the peak and the trough. In an f-string, {peak:%b %Y} prints a date as “Dec 2005”, and {change:+.1f} a number with its sign. On a ratio (log) axis, Plotly wants the axis range as powers of ten, so we pass np.log10(...). With xref="paper" and yref="paper", a label’s position is a share of the plot area (0 = left or bottom, 1 = right or top), not a date or a value.

BUSTS = {"1970s boom and bust": ("1977-01-01", "1985-12-01"),
         "1980s boom and bust": ("1986-01-01", "1997-12-01"),
         "2000s boom and bust": ("2000-01-01", "2015-12-01"),
         "2020s so far": ("2021-01-01", "2026-07-01")}


def housing_chart(bust="2000s boom and bust"):
    """Fig. 10.1: the real home price index (ratio scale), with one boom and bust shaded."""
    start, end = BUSTS[bust]
    peak, trough, change = peak_to_trough(house, start, end)
    fig = px.line(housing, x="date", y="real_home_price_index", log_y=True,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "real_home_price_index": "Real home prices (1953 = 100)"},
                  title=f"{bust}: real home prices fell {-change:.1f}% from {peak:%b %Y} to {trough:%b %Y}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=TEAL, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak, trough], y=[house[peak], house[trough]], mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11), showlegend=False, name="Peak and trough"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=0.02, y=0.97, xref="paper", yref="paper", xanchor="left", yanchor="top", showarrow=False,
                       text=f"Shaded: {peak:%b %Y} to {trough:%b %Y}<br>real prices {change:+.1f}%", font=dict(size=13))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=["1952-01-01", "2027-06-01"])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200], range=[np.log10(84), np.log10(250)])
    return fig

Python note. interact calls housing_chart and shows the figure it returns. bust=Dropdown(...) turns the argument bust into a menu (list(BUSTS) gives the names in the dictionary), and the figure is drawn again each time you pick an episode. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(housing_chart, bust=Dropdown(options=list(BUSTS), value="2000s boom and bust",
                                      description="boom and bust", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with a precomputed slider for the boom and bust
slider_figure(housing_chart, "bust", ["1970s boom and bust", "1980s boom and bust", "2000s boom and bust",
                                      "2020s so far"], start="2000s boom and bust", label="episode")

Sources. Data: Robert J. Shiller, U.S. Home Price and Related Data, real home price index (from 1987 the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index, deflated by the BLS consumer price index). Prepared file: data/ch10/fig10-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Real house prices hardly changed for 45 years: the index was still near 100 in the late 1990s. Then it rose steeply to a peak of 171 in December 2005 and fell by 35.7 percent to February 2012.
  • Choose the 1970s and 1980s episodes: those busts were 12.2 and 14.4 percent, less than half of the 2006–2012 bust. That is why the textbook calls the decline after 2006 “by far the largest” since 1953.
  • On a ratio scale, equal distances are equal percentage changes, so the busts of different decades can be compared by eye. Since 2022 the index has stayed close to its new record (choose “2020s so far”).

Key numbers: the bubble in numbers

The textbook gives three numbers: a decline of 36 percent from the middle of 2006 to the first quarter of 2012, a next-largest decline of 14 percent, and a rise “by a factor of nearly 3 between 1996 and 2006”. house.cummax() is the highest value reached so far, so house / house.cummax() - 1 is the fall from the latest record, called the drawdown.

drawdown = 100 * (house / house.cummax() - 1)
print(f"Largest drawdown since 1953: {drawdown.min():.1f}% in {drawdown.idxmin():%b %Y}")
mid_2006, early_2012 = house["2006-04-01":"2006-06-01"].mean(), house["2012-01-01":"2012-03-01"].mean()
print(f"2006Q2 to 2012Q1 (quarterly averages): {percent_change(early_2012, mid_2006):.1f}%")
factor = house["2006"].mean() / house["1996"].mean()
print(f"1996 to 2006 (annual averages): prices x {factor:.2f}, or {100 * (factor ** (1 / 10) - 1):.1f}% a year")
Largest drawdown since 1953: -35.7% in Feb 2012
2006Q2 to 2012Q1 (quarterly averages): -35.1%
1996 to 2006 (annual averages): prices x 1.72, or 5.6% a year

The first two numbers match the textbook. The third does not: in this real index, prices rose by a factor of 1.72 between 1996 and 2006, or 5.6 percent a year (equation 2), not “nearly 3” and “about 10 percent per year”. The textbook’s prose probably uses another index (for example nominal prices, or a 20-city index with the booming coastal markets). Always check which series a number comes from.

Beyond the U.S.: house prices in other countries

Was the U.S. bubble unusual? The BIS publishes real residential property prices (house prices divided by the consumer price index) for about 60 economies, quarterly, as an index with 2010 = 100. For the U.S. the BIS uses a different house-price index than Shiller, but it tells the same story: a fall of 38.9 percent from the 2006 peak, against Shiller’s 35.3 percent in quarterly averages.

house_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "house_prices_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
house_panel.tail(3)
iso3 country date real_house_price
8838 USA United States 2025-10-01 158.21
8839 USA United States 2026-01-01 156.53
8840 USA United States 2026-04-01 154.21

Python note. SelectMultiple is a list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click. It hands the function a tuple of names, such as ("United States", "Spain"). color="country" draws one line per country, and color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS gives each its fixed color.

def house_world(names=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 10.1 beyond the U.S.: BIS real house prices (2010 = 100, ratio scale) in the chosen countries."""
    chosen, missing = pick(house_panel, names, "real_house_price")
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="date", y="real_house_price", color="country", log_y=True, hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "real_house_price": "Real house prices (2010 = 100)", "country": "Country"})
    worst = largest_fall(chosen, "real_house_price", "2000-01-01", "2015-12-31")
    title = "No data between 2000 and 2015"
    if worst is not None:
        name, peak, trough, change = worst
        title = (f"Largest 2000–15 bust: {name}, {change:.1f}% "
                 f"({peak.year}Q{peak.quarter} to {trough.year}Q{trough.quarter})")
    fig.update_layout(title=title + no_data_note(missing))
    return fig
interact(house_world, names=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(house_panel.country.unique()), value=("United States",),
                                           rows=8, description="countries"));

Sources. Data: Bank for International Settlements, residential property prices, real (dataset WS_SPP), BIS data portal, compiled from national sources; the same series are on FRED, e.g. U.S. real residential property prices (QUSR628BIS). Prepared files: data/ch10/house_prices_panel.csv, data/ch10/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Click a country in the legend to add it, or choose a region in the menu.

What to notice.

  • The title reports the U.S. bust in the BIS data: 38.9 percent from 2006Q1 to 2011Q3. Add Ireland and Spain: their real house prices fell by 56.7 and 44.5 percent after 2007, more than in the U.S. Both had banking crises too.
  • Add Germany and Japan: real house prices in Germany fell slowly for three decades, by 30.8 percent from 1981 to 2010, and Japan’s bubble burst in 1991, long before the U.S. one. Not every country had a boom in the 2000s.
  • Data hygiene. The series start in different years (Italy in 1947, Poland in 2010), so check the first date of a country before you compare long-run changes.

Your turn. How many months did it take, after the trough of February 2012, for real house prices to climb back above their December 2005 peak?

Hint

Keep the months after the trough that are above the peak: house["2012-02-01":][house["2012-02-01":] > house["2005-12-01"]]. The first date of the result (.index[0]) is the answer.

Fig. 2: The Fed funds rate

Goal. Follow the Federal Reserve’s main interest rate through the boom, the crisis and the pandemic.

The Fed funds rate is the interest rate banks charge one another for overnight loans. The Federal Reserve sets a target for it, and the data show the effective rate, the monthly average of what banks actually paid.

fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig10-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fed_rate = fed.set_index("date").fed_funds
fed.head()
date fed_funds
0 2000-01-01 5.45
1 2000-02-01 5.73
2 2000-03-01 5.85
3 2000-04-01 6.02
4 2000-05-01 6.27

Four periods tell the story. The menu zooms in on one of them, and the title reports the lowest and highest rate in that window.

Python note. px.area draws a line with the area below it filled in. fig.update_xaxes(range=[a, b]) sets the dates shown. shade_recessions(fig) is our function from “Model overview”.

PERIODS = {"2000–2026": ("2000-01-01", "2026-09-01"),
           "2004–06 hikes": ("2003-06-01", "2007-06-01"),
           "2007–08 cuts": ("2007-06-01", "2009-06-01"),
           "2022–23 hikes": ("2021-06-01", "2024-06-01")}


def fed_chart(period="2000–2026"):
    """Fig. 10.2: the effective Fed funds rate, with recessions shaded, over one period."""
    start, end = PERIODS[period]
    window = fed_rate[start:end]
    low, high = window.idxmin(), window.idxmax()
    fig = px.area(fed, x="date", y="fed_funds", labels={"date": "Year", "fed_funds": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{period}: lowest {window[low]:.2f}% ({low:%b %Y}), highest {window[high]:.2f}% ({high:%b %Y})")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fillcolor="rgba(138, 150, 163, 0.3)")
    shade_recessions(fig)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[pd.Timestamp(start) - pd.DateOffset(months=6), pd.Timestamp(end) + pd.DateOffset(months=3)])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 8], tickvals=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])   # no 0 label: it would crowd the first year
    return fig
interact(fed_chart, period=Dropdown(options=list(PERIODS), value="2000–2026", description="period", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version

    buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="relayout",
                        args=[{"xaxis.range": list(zoomed.layout.xaxis.range), "title.text": zoomed.layout.title.text}]))

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; NBER recession dates (USREC), via FRED. Prepared files: data/ch10/fig10-2.csv, data/ch10/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • After the 2001 recession, the Fed kept the rate at about 1 percent until mid-2004, then raised it step by step to above 5 percent by mid-2006. Higher rates made mortgages more expensive just as house prices peaked.
  • From August 2007 the Fed cut, and by December 2008 the rate was close to zero. It stayed there for seven years: zero is a floor for interest rates, the zero lower bound of Chapters 11 and 14.
  • In 2020 the rate went back to zero. In 2022 the Fed raised it again, quickly, to fight inflation (Fig. 10), to 5.33 percent by August 2023.

Key numbers: target rates and effective rates

The textbook says that between May 2004 and May 2006 the Fed raised its rate “from 1.25 percent to 5.25 percent”.

for month in ["2004-05-01", "2004-07-01", "2006-05-01", "2006-07-01"]:
    print(f"{pd.Timestamp(month):%b %Y}: {fed_rate[month]:.2f}%")
print(f"Highest rate from Jan 2009 to Nov 2015: {fed_rate['2009-01-01':'2015-11-01'].max():.2f}%")
print(f"Dec 2015: {fed_rate['2015-12-01']:.2f}%   Latest ({fed_rate.index[-1]:%b %Y}): {fed_rate.iloc[-1]:.2f}%")
May 2004: 1.00%
Jul 2004: 1.26%
May 2006: 4.94%
Jul 2006: 5.24%
Highest rate from Jan 2009 to Nov 2015: 0.22%
Dec 2015: 0.24%   Latest (Sep 2026): 3.75%

The textbook’s numbers are the Fed’s targets. The effective rate follows the target with a short delay: 1.00 percent in May 2004 and 4.94 percent in May 2006, and 1.26 and 5.24 percent two months later. From January 2009 to November 2015 the rate never rose above 0.22 percent, and it first moved up in December 2015.

Beyond the U.S.: central bank policy rates

Every central bank has a policy rate like the Fed’s. The BIS collects them for 41 economies, as the rate in force at the end of each month. For the U.S. the BIS uses the middle of the Fed’s target range, so its line steps where the effective rate of Fig. 2 moves smoothly; the two differ by 0.04 points in a typical month.

rates_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "policy_rates_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
rates_panel.tail(3)
iso3 country date policy_rate
12410 USA United States 2026-07-01 3.625
12411 USA United States 2026-08-01 3.625
12412 USA United States 2026-09-01 3.875

The title measures the rate hikes of 2021–24 with largest_rise: the rise from the lowest rate to the highest later rate, in percentage points.

Python note. line_shape="hv" draws each line as steps (horizontal, then vertical), because a policy rate stays put until the central bank changes it. fig.add_hline(y=0, ...) draws a horizontal line at zero.

def policy_world(names=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 10.2 beyond the U.S.: BIS central bank policy rates (end of month) in the chosen countries."""
    chosen, missing = pick(rates_panel, names, "policy_rate")
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="date", y="policy_rate", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS, line_shape="hv",          # rates change in steps
                  labels={"date": "Year", "policy_rate": "Policy rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    most = largest_rise(chosen, "policy_rate", "2021-01-01", "2024-12-31")
    title = "No data for 2021–24"
    if most is not None:
        name, low, high, rise = most
        title = f"Largest 2021–24 hike: {name}, +{rise:.2f} points ({low:%b %Y} to {high:%b %Y})"
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=title + no_data_note(missing))
    return fig

Sources. Data: Bank for International Settlements, central bank policy rates (dataset WS_CBPOL), BIS data portal. Prepared files: data/ch10/policy_rates_panel.csv, data/ch10/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Click a country in the legend to add it, or choose a region in the menu.

What to notice.

  • Add the euro area and the United Kingdom: like the Fed, the Bank of England and the European Central Bank cut to almost zero after 2008 and raised their rates in 2022–23, by 5.15 and 4.50 points.
  • Add Switzerland and Japan: their policy rates were negative for years (Switzerland −0.75 percent from 2015), so zero is not quite a floor. Banks paid the central bank to hold their reserves.
  • Add Brazil or Türkiye: emerging economies raised rates much more (+11.75 and +41.5 points), because their inflation was much higher. The y-axis widens to fit them.
  • Data hygiene. The euro area never goes below zero here, although the ECB charged −0.5 percent on deposits from 2019 to 2022: until September 2024 the BIS uses the ECB’s main refinancing rate, and from then on its deposit rate. A series can change its definition in the middle.

Fig. 3: Liquidity and risk shocks from interest rate spreads

Goal. See the financial crisis in the price banks paid to borrow from one another.

The TED spread is the 3-month LIBOR rate (what banks charged one another) minus the 3-month Treasury bill rate (what the U.S. government pays). Lending to the government is safe, so the spread is a risk premium: it rises when banks fear that other banks might not repay (equation 10). LIBOR was discontinued in 2022, so the data file adds a second, similar spread that continues: AA-rated financial commercial paper minus the Treasury bill.

spreads = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig10-3.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
spread = spreads.set_index("date")
spreads[spreads.isna().any(axis=1)].head(3)
date ted_spread cp_tbill_spread
243 2020-04-01 0.9605 NaN
265 2022-02-01 NaN 0.055044
266 2022-03-01 NaN 0.288101

NaN (“not a number”) marks a missing value, and spreads.isna().any(axis=1) is true for the rows with at least one missing value, so the cell shows the first three of them. The TED spread stops in January 2022, and the commercial-paper spread has one gap, April 2020, when the Federal Reserve published no commercial-paper rate. Plotly simply leaves a small gap in the line.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. fig.add_annotation writes a label with an arrow that points at a data point; ax and ay set where the label sits, in pixels from that point.

named = spreads.rename(columns={"ted_spread": "TED spread: LIBOR minus T-bill",
                                "cp_tbill_spread": "Commercial paper minus T-bill"})
peak_date = spread.ted_spread.idxmax()
fig = px.line(named, x="date", y=["TED spread: LIBOR minus T-bill", "Commercial paper minus T-bill"],
              color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL],
              labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percentage points", "variable": "Spread"},
              title=f"Banks stopped trusting each other: the TED spread reached {spread.ted_spread.max():.2f} points")
fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="TED spread: LIBOR minus T-bill"), line_width=3)
fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Commercial paper minus T-bill"), line_width=1.5)
fig.add_annotation(x=peak_date, y=spread.ted_spread.max(), text=f"Lehman Brothers fails:<br>{peak_date:%B %Y}",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=90, ay=10, font=dict(size=13))
shade_recessions(fig)
fig.update_xaxes(range=["1999-07-01", "2026-12-01"])
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 3.6], tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5])
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
fig.show()

Sources. Data: ICE Benchmark Administration and Federal Reserve Board, TED Spread (TEDRATE), via FRED; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 90-Day AA Financial Commercial Paper Interest Rate (RIFSPPFAAD90NB), via FRED; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 3-Month Treasury Bill Secondary Market Rate (DTB3), via FRED; NBER recession dates (USREC), via FRED. Prepared files: data/ch10/fig10-3.csv, data/ch10/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Before the crisis the spread was small and calm. It jumped in August 2007, when banks first doubted one another, and exploded in the autumn of 2008, after Lehman Brothers failed in September.
  • The two spreads move closely together, so the commercial-paper spread is a good stand-in after 2022. Click a spread in the legend to hide it.
  • Covid-19 also caused a spike in March 2020, but a short one: the Federal Reserve quickly lent to the markets. Since 2022 there has been no stress episode like 2007–08.

Key numbers: three phases of the crisis

ted = spread.ted_spread
calm, stress = ted["2002-01-01":"2007-07-01"], ted["2007-08-01":"2008-08-01"]
print(f"Jan 2002 - Jul 2007: average {calm.mean():.2f}, range {calm.min():.2f} to {calm.max():.2f} points")
print(f"Aug 2007 - Aug 2008: average {stress.mean():.2f}, range {stress.min():.2f} to {stress.max():.2f} points")
print(f"Peak: {ted.max():.2f} points in {ted.idxmax():%b %Y}")
print(f"Correlation of the two spreads, 2000-2022: {spread.ted_spread.corr(spread.cp_tbill_spread):.2f}")
recent = spread.cp_tbill_spread["2022-02-01":]
print(f"Commercial-paper spread since Feb 2022: highest {recent.max():.2f} points ({recent.idxmax():%b %Y})")
Jan 2002 - Jul 2007: average 0.33, range 0.16 to 0.75 points
Aug 2007 - Aug 2008: average 1.31, range 0.91 to 2.00 points
Peak: 3.35 points in Oct 2008
Correlation of the two spreads, 2000-2022: 0.97
Commercial-paper spread since Feb 2022: highest 0.38 points (Jun 2022)

The textbook’s “modest premium of 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points” is the calm phase, on average 0.33 points. From August 2007 the spread averaged 1.31 points, close to the textbook’s “between 1.0 and 1.5”. The textbook’s “more than 4.5 percentage points” refers to single days in October 2008: monthly averages, as in our file, smooth the spike to 3.35 points.

Beyond the U.S.: stress in other money markets

The TED spread exists only in U.S. dollars, and LIBOR is gone. But the OECD publishes two money-market rates for 35 economies: a 3-month interbank rate (a 3-month loan between banks, like LIBOR) and an overnight interbank rate (a one-day loan, which follows the policy rate). Their difference is a risk premium too: a bank that lends for three months instead of one day fears more that the borrower fails. It is not the TED spread, and it also moves when banks expect the policy rate to change. For the U.S. it peaks in the same month as the TED spread, October 2008, but at 2.22 instead of 3.35 points.

spreads_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "interbank_spreads_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
spreads_panel.tail(3)
iso3 country date interbank_3m overnight spread

9324 USA United States 2026-08-01 3.82 3.630 0.190
9325 USA United States 2026-09-01 3.94 3.742 0.198

The euro-area countries share the euro area’s money-market rates once they adopt the euro, so the file keeps them only for the years when they had rates of their own (Greece in 2000, for example); choose “Euro area” for the rest.

Python note. chosen.date.dt.year.between(2007, 2009) is true for the dates in the years 2007 to 2009. crisis.spread.idxmax() is the row label of the largest spread, and crisis.loc[...] picks that whole row, so top.country and top.date say where and when it happened.

def spread_world(names=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 10.3 beyond the U.S.: 3-month interbank rate minus the overnight rate, in the chosen countries."""
    chosen, missing = pick(spreads_panel, names, "spread")
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="date", y="spread", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "spread": "Spread (percentage points)", "country": "Country"})
    crisis = chosen[chosen.date.dt.year.between(2007, 2009)]
    title = "No data for 2007–09"
    if len(crisis) > 0:
        top = crisis.loc[crisis.spread.idxmax()]                 # the row with the largest spread
        title = f"Largest spread in 2007–09: {top.country}, {top.spread:.2f} points ({top.date:%b %Y})"
    shade_recessions(fig)
    fig.update_layout(title=title + no_data_note(missing))
    return fig
interact(spread_world, names=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(spreads_panel.country.unique()), value=("United States",),
                                            rows=8, description="countries"));

Prepared files: data/ch10/interbank_spreads_panel.csv, data/ch10/countries.csv, data/ch10/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 10.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Click a country in the legend to add it, or choose a region in the menu. The shaded bands are U.S. recessions.

What to notice.

  • Add the euro area and the United Kingdom: their spreads also jumped in August 2007 and peaked in October 2008, at 1.29 and 1.72 points. The crisis spread through the money markets of the whole world at once.
  • Add Canada: its spread hardly moved (at most 0.11 points in 2007–09). Canada’s banks were not hit by the crisis.
  • Data hygiene. Add Russia and Romania: in their currency crises the spread reaches 14.8 points (Russia, January
    1. and 19.6 points (Romania, March 2000), and Russia’s falls to −27 points in 2000. An overnight rate can spike when a central bank defends its currency, so a large negative spread here is not a sign of calm.

CRASHES = {"Dot-com bust, 2000–03": ("1999-01-01", "2003-12-01"),
           "Financial crisis, 2007–09": ("2007-01-01", "2009-12-01"),
           "Covid-19, 2020": ("2020-01-01", "2020-06-01"),     # ends before prices pass the January peak
           "Rate hikes, 2022": ("2021-06-01", "2022-12-01")}


def stock_chart(crash="Financial crisis, 2007–09"):
    """Fig. 10.4: the real S&P 500 (ratio scale), with one crash shaded and measured."""
    start, end = CRASHES[crash]
    peak, trough, change = peak_to_trough(sp500, start, end)
    fig = px.area(stocks, x="date", y="sp500_real", log_y=True,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "sp500_real": "Real stock price index (ratio scale)"},
                  title=f"{crash}: real stock prices fell {-change:.1f}% from {peak:%b %Y} to {trough:%b %Y}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fillcolor="rgba(138, 150, 163, 0.3)")
    fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak, trough], y=[sp500[peak], sp500[trough]], mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10), showlegend=False, name="Peak and trough"))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=["1989-07-01", "2027-06-01"])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[640, 1280, 2560, 5120, 10240], range=[np.log10(700), np.log10(9500)])
    return fig
